mature_ideas.title: Operational Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures Under High-Power-Density Thermal Cycling
mature_ideas.hypothesis: Random interlayer rotations engineered to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: Random interlayer rotations engineered to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.
mature_ideas.scientific_object: Twisted multilayer van der Waals heterostructures (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) with controlled interlayer rotation angles
mature_ideas.mechanism: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder

mature_ideas.falsifier: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking within device-relevant thermal cycling conditions (e.g., 1000 cycles between 300 K and 500 K), resulting in recovery of cross-plane conductivity to within 20% of pristine aligned values

mature_ideas.title: Dynamic Twist Angle Tuning via Strain-Mediated Moiré Potential Modulation
mature_ideas.hypothesis: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_ideas.mechanism: Apply controlled biaxial strain to twisted van der Waals heterostructures while measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity. Use piezoelectric actuators or thermal expansion mismatch to modulate strain dynamically. Correlate strain-induced moiré potential changes with thermal conductivity variations. This tests whether twist-angle engineering can be made adaptive rather than static.

mature_ideas.title: Quantitative Crossover Boundary from Bulk-Dominated to Interface-Dominated Thermal Resistance in Heterogeneous Interfaces Under High Power Density
mature_ideas.hypothesis: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable critical interface bonding energy threshold that scales with the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length, and this threshold shifts under high-power-density conditions due to non-equilibrium phonon population effects.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable critical interface bonding energy threshold that scales with the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length, and this threshold shifts under high-power-density conditions due to non-equilibrium phonon population effects.
mature_ideas.scientific_object: Heterogeneous material interfaces (metal-semiconductor, dielectric-substrate, van der Waals junctions) with systematically varied bonding strength and contamination levels
mature_ideas.mechanism: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

assumptions: Interface transmission probability can be parameterized by a single effective bonding energy metric
Bulk phonon mean free path distribution remains invariant under moderate power density increases
Non-equilibrium optical phonon populations do not significantly alter interface transmission coefficients
The crossover threshold is material-pair specific but follows predictable scaling laws

SURVEY_ANCHOR: 'interfacial thermal resistance frequently imposes the dominant bottleneck in nanoscale systems, particularly when the characteristic length scales approach or fall below the phonon mean free path'

mature_ideas.title: Discriminating Observation Protocol for Partitioning Phonon vs. Electron Heat Conduction Contributions in High-Power-Density Materials
mature_ideas.hypothesis: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials can be discriminated by exploiting the differential response of each carrier type to controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, combined with spectral phonon imaging to directly visualize phonon transport pathways.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials can be discriminated by exploiting the differential response of each carrier type to controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, combined with spectral phonon imaging to directly visualize phonon transport pathways.
mature_ideas.scientific_object: High-power-density materials (wide-bandgap semiconductors, doped thermoelectrics, metallic thin films) under controlled carrier density and temperature gradients
mature_ideas.mechanism: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
mature_ideas.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
assumptions: Wiedemann-Franz law deviations can be attributed primarily to electron-phonon coupling rather than other scattering mechanisms
Spectral phonon imaging has sufficient resolution to distinguish phonon contributions from electron contributions
Carrier density variations do not significantly alter phonon dispersion or scattering rates
The material system allows independent control of carrier density without introducing additional defect scattering
evidence_basis: SURVEY_ANCHOR: 'No discriminating observation exists to separate phonon vs. electron heat conduction contributions to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials'
SURVEY_ANCHOR: 'What evidence distinguishes the relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to the maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials?'
SURVEY_ANCHOR: 'No discriminating observation differentiates phonon-mediated from electron-mediated heat conduction contributions under comparable high-power-density conditions'
mature_ideas.refinement_scope: Develop and validate a discriminating observation protocol that can partition phonon and electron heat conduction contributions under high-power-density conditions, addressing the identifiability gap in the survey
mature_ideas.falsifier: Demonstration that phonon and electron contributions cannot be independently varied or measured with sufficient precision to distinguish their relative contributions, or that Wiedemann-Franz deviations are dominated by mechanisms other than electron-phonon coupling
